text: planar angle \(\theta\) point defined ratio arc length radius: \[\theta = \frac{l}{r}\] \(l\) arc length circle radius \(r\). full circle subtends \(2\pi\) radians, establishing normalization angular measure two dimensions. definition extends naturally higher dimensions concept solid angles. colinear opposite rays, cone degenerates line normalized measure 0 (0.5).
code: #### Quarter circle (90 degrees = \u03C0/2 radians)                       #### v1 <- c(1, 0) v2 <- c(0, 1) V_90 <- cbind(v1, v2)  omega_90 <- solid_angle_2d(v1, v2) planar_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Normalized measure", "Absolute angle (radians)"),   value = c(omega_90, omega_90 * 2 * pi),   expected = c(0.25, pi/2) ) knitr::kable(   planar_table,   digits = c(NA, 4, 4),   col.names = c("quantity", "value", "expected") )

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: solid angle \(\Omega\) quantifies three-dimensional angular extent subtended object point. Analogous planar angles, defined : \[\Omega = \frac{}{r^2}\] \(\) surface area projected onto sphere radius \(r\) centered observation point. unit solid angle steradian (sr), dimensionless quantity \(\text{sr} = \text{rad}^2\). Key properties: complete sphere subtends \(\Omega = 4\pi\) steradians; hemisphere subtends \(\Omega = 2\pi\) steradians; orthant (one-eighth sphere) subtends \(\Omega = \frac{\pi}{2}\) steradians. differential solid angle spherical coordinates \((\theta, \varphi)\) : \[d\Omega = \sin\theta \, d\theta \, d\varphi\] \(\theta \[0, \pi]\) polar angle \(\varphi \[0, 2\pi]\) azimuthal angle. arbitrary oriented surface \(S\), solid angle computed via surface integral: \[\Omega = \iint_S \frac{\hat{r} \cdot \hat{n}}{r^2} \, dS\] \(\hat{r}\) unit vector observation point surface element \(\hat{n}\) unit normal.
code: #### Orthant (positive octant)                                           #### V_octant <- diag(3)  omega_octant <- solid_angle_3d(V_octant[, 1], V_octant[, 2], V_octant[, 3]) octant_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Normalized measure", "Absolute solid angle (sr)"),   value = c(omega_octant, omega_octant * 4 * pi),   expected = c(0.125, pi/2) ) knitr::kable(   octant_table,   digits = c(NA, 6, 6),   col.names = c("quantity", "value", "expected") )

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: right circular cone apex origin half-apex angle \(\theta\), solid angle elegant closed form: \[\boxed{\Omega_{\text{cone}} = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta)}\] Derivation: cone intersects unit sphere circle colatitude \(\theta\). solid angle equals area spherical cap: \[\Omega = \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\theta \sin\theta' \, d\theta' \, d\varphi = 2\pi[-\cos\theta']_0^\theta = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta)\] small angles, \(\Omega \approx \pi\theta^2\), recovering intuitive result solid angle scales square angular extent.
code: #### Test circular cone formula                                          #### theta_values <- c(pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2) theta_degrees <- theta_values * 180 / pi  cone_table <- data.frame(   theta_deg = theta_degrees,   omega_normalized = solid_angle_cone(theta_values),   formula = (1 - cos(theta_values)) / 2 ) knitr::kable(   cone_table,   digits = c(1, 6, 6),   col.names = c("theta (deg)", "omega (normalized)", "formula") )

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: spherical triangle formed three great circular arcs sphere’s surface. Unlike planar triangles, spherical triangles exhibit positive spherical excess: sum interior angles exceeds \(\pi\). Let \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\) denote interior angles \(, b, c\) opposite side lengths (measured arc lengths). spherical excess \(E\) defined : \[E = \alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi\]

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: Theorem (Girard, 1626 [9]): area \(\) spherical triangle sphere radius \(R\) equals \(R^2\) times spherical excess: \[\boxed{= R^2(\alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi) = R^2 E}\] unit sphere (\(R = 1\)), area equals excess directly. profound result connects intrinsic geometry (angles) extrinsic geometry (area). Proof sketch: Consider three lunes (double wedges) formed extending side complete great circle. lune angle \(\psi\) area \(4\psi R^2\). three lunes cover sphere cover triangle antipodal image three times : \[4\alpha R^2 + 4\beta R^2 + 4\gamma R^2 = 4\pi R^2 + 6A\] Simplifying yields Girard’s formula. Since solid angle unit sphere equals area, : \[\boxed{\Omega_{\text{triangle}} = \alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi}\] establishes fundamental connection solid angles spherical geometry.
code: #### Right spherical triangle (all angles = 90\u00B0)                     #### #### Each angle is \u03C0/2, so E = 3(\u03C0/2) - \u03C0 = \u03C0/2                       #### v1 <- c(1, 0, 0) v2 <- c(0, 1, 0) v3 <- c(0, 0, 1)  E_measured <- spherical_triangle_area(v1, v2, v3) E_girard <- 3 * (pi/2) - pi  # All angles are 90\u00B0 girard_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Measured area (sr)", "Girard's formula (sr)", "Normalized solid angle"),   value = c(E_measured, E_girard, E_measured / (4 * pi)) ) knitr::kable(   girard_table,   digits = c(NA, 6),   col.names = c("quantity", "value") )

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: Theorem (L’Huilier, 1789 [11]): spherical triangle sides \(, b, c\) semiperimeter \(s = \frac{+b+c}{2}\), spherical excess satisfies: \[\boxed{\tan\left(\frac{E}{4}\right) = \sqrt{\tan\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\tan\left(\frac{s-}{2}\right)\tan\left(\frac{s-b}{2}\right)\tan\left(\frac{s-c}{2}\right)}}\] spherical analogue Heron’s formula, enabling area computation side lengths alone without computing angles first. computational advantage makes L’Huilier’s theorem particularly valuable numerical applications.
code: #### Equilateral spherical triangle                                      #### a <- b <- c <- pi/3  # 60-degree sides  E_lhuilier <- lhuilier_angle(a, b, c) lhuilier_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Spherical excess (sr)", "Normalized solid angle"),   value = c(E_lhuilier, E_lhuilier / (4 * pi)) ) knitr::kable(   lhuilier_table,   digits = c(NA, 6),   col.names = c("quantity", "value") ) #### For small triangles, compare with Euclidean Heron's formula         #### a_small <- b_small <- c_small <- 0.1 E_small <- lhuilier_angle(a_small, b_small, c_small)  #### Heron's formula for planar triangle                                 #### s_planar <- (a_small + b_small + c_small) / 2 area_planar <- sqrt(s_planar * (s_planar - a_small) * (s_planar - b_small) *                     (s_planar - c_small))  small_triangle_table <- data.frame(   quantity = c("Spherical (L'Huilier)", "Planar (Heron)", "Relative difference"),   value = c(E_small, area_planar, abs(E_small - area_planar) / area_planar) ) knitr::kable(   small_triangle_table,   digits = c(NA, 8),   col.names = c("quantity", "value") )

text: Spherical law cosines (sides): \[\cos c = \cos \cos b + \sin \sin b \cos \Gamma\] \(\Gamma\) angle opposite side \(c\). Spherical law cosines (angles): \[\cos \Gamma = -\cos \cos B + \sin \sin B \cos c\] Spherical law sines: \[\frac{\sin }{\sin } = \frac{\sin b}{\sin B} = \frac{\sin c}{\sin C}\] Right spherical triangles (\(\Gamma = \pi/2\)) satisfy spherical Pythagorean theorem: \[\cos c = \cos \cos b\] laws, developed extensively Euler [10] Lagrange 18th century using variational methods, form foundation spherical angle computations.

text: 1983, Van Oosterom Strackee [5] published landmark formula solid angle subtended plane triangle, resolving longstanding computational challenge. Theorem (Van Oosterom-Strackee, 1983 [5]): Let \(\vec{r}_1, \vec{r}_2, \vec{r}_3\) position vectors observation point vertices triangle. solid angle subtended : \[\boxed{\tan\left(\frac{\Omega}{2}\right) = \frac{[\vec{r}_1 \, \vec{r}_2 \, \vec{r}_3]}{r_1 r_2 r_3 + (\vec{r}_1 \cdot \vec{r}_2)r_3 + (\vec{r}_1 \cdot \vec{r}_3)r_2 + (\vec{r}_2 \cdot \vec{r}_3)r_1}}\] \([\vec{r}_1 \, \vec{r}_2 \, \vec{r}_3] = \vec{r}_1 \cdot (\vec{r}_2 \times \vec{r}_3)\) scalar triple product \(r_i = |\vec{r}_i|\).

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: polyhedral cone defined \(n\) unit vectors \(\{\mathbf{s}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{s}_n\}\) (cyclic order), Mazonka derives remarkably efficient formula using complex arithmetic. Define vertex \(j\): \[a_j = \mathbf{s}_j \cdot \mathbf{s}_{j-1}, \quad b_j = \mathbf{s}_j \cdot \mathbf{s}_{j+1}\] \[c_j = \mathbf{s}_j \cdot (\mathbf{s}_{j-1} \times \mathbf{s}_{j+1})\] \[d_j = [\mathbf{s}_{j-1}, \mathbf{s}_j, \mathbf{s}_{j+1}] = \mathbf{s}_{j-1} \cdot (\mathbf{s}_j \times \mathbf{s}_{j+1})\] Main formula: \[\boxed{\Omega = 2\pi - \arg\left\{\prod_{j=1}^{n} (cb_j - a_j + d_j )\right\}}\] product complex numbers \(z_j = (cb_j - a_j) + d_j \). Key advantage: requires one arctangent operation (final argument), compared one per vertex traditional methods. Complexity O(n) constants dominated vector operations, transcendental functions.

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: \(n=3\) (triangular face), \(d_j\) equal: \(d_1 = d_2 = d_3 = d\). allows factorization: \[\Omega = 2\pi - \arg[(bc-+di)(ac-b+di)(ab-c+di)]\] Using \(d^2 = 1 + 2abc - ^2 - b^2 - c^2\) simplifying: \[\Omega = 2\pi - 2\arg[(1++b+c) + di]\] Therefore: \[\boxed{\tan\frac{\Omega}{2} = \frac{d}{1++b+c}}\] exactly recovers Van Oosterom-Strackee formula, demonstrating Mazonka’s approach unifies extends classical results.

title: A mathematical introduction to solid angle methods for polyhedral cones with the SolidAngleR library
text: Mazonka addresses problem covered series methods: computing solid angle intersection two cones apertures \(\theta_1, \theta_2\) axes separated angle \(\alpha\). Geometric construction: cone intersects unit sphere circle (spherical cap boundary); two circles intersect two points; plane intersection points cuts cap segments; total intersection solid angle equals sum two cap segments. Determining \(\gamma_1\): Using spherical trigonometry right triangles formed, robust form : \[\boxed{\gamma_1 = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left(\cos\alpha \cos\theta_1 - \cos\theta_2,\; \sin\alpha \cos\theta_1\right)}\] analogously \(\gamma_2\) (swap indices). \(\operatorname{atan2}\) form preserves sign quadrant information can lost plain \(\tan^{-1}\) expression. Total intersection: \[\boxed{\Omega_{\text{int}} = \Omega(\theta_1, \gamma_1) + \Omega(\theta_2, \gamma_2)}\] provides closed-form solution acute cones; practical implementations also handle special cases (hemispheres, containment, opposite axes) may fall back robust spherical-cap overlap integral analytic formula ill-conditioned.

code: # Create a cone that can be computed both ways theta <- pi/3 n_sides <- 8  # Approximate circular cone with octagonal cone  # Create octagonal cone vertices angles <- seq(0, 2*pi, length.out = n_sides + 1)[-(n_sides + 1)] radius <- sin(theta) height <- cos(theta)  vertices_octagon <- rbind(   radius * cos(angles),   radius * sin(angles),   rep(height, n_sides) )  # Normalize to unit sphere vertices_octagon <- apply(vertices_octagon, 2, function(v) v / sqrt(sum(v^2)))  # Method 1: Geometric (circular cone) omega_geometric <- solid_angle_cone(theta)  # Method 2: Polyhedral (average over faces) omega_polyhedral_faces <- numeric(n_sides) for (i in 1:n_sides) {   j <- ifelse(i == n_sides, 1, i + 1)   face <- cbind(c(0, 0, 1), vertices_octagon[, i], vertices_octagon[, j])   omega_polyhedral_faces[i] <- solid_angle_polyhedral(face) } omega_polyhedral <- sum(omega_polyhedral_faces)  # Method 3: Algebraic (using 3D formula on apex vectors) # Create matrix from cone apex_vec <- c(0, 0, 1) V_cone <- cbind(apex_vec, vertices_octagon[, 1:2]) omega_algebraic <- solid_angle_3d(V_cone[, 1], V_cone[, 2], V_cone[, 3])  comparison_table <- data.frame(   method = c(     "Geometric (exact)",     sprintf("Polyhedral (%d-sided)", n_sides),     "Algebraic (3 vectors)"   ),   omega_normalized = c(omega_geometric, omega_polyhedral, omega_algebraic),   abs_error = c(0, abs(omega_polyhedral - omega_geometric),                 abs(omega_algebraic - omega_geometric)) ) knitr::kable(   comparison_table,   digits = c(NA, 6, 2),   col.names = c("method", "omega (normalized)", "abs. error") )

what: Monte Carlo integration on the sphere
title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: solid angle \(\Omega\) subtended region \(\mathcal{R}\) unit sphere \(S^2\) defined : \[\Omega = \int_{\mathcal{R}} dS\] \(dS\) differential surface area element. measurable region characteristic function \(\chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x})\) (equals 1 \(\mathbf{x} \\mathcal{R}\), 0 otherwise): \[\Omega = \int_{S^2} \chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x}) \, dS\] Monte Carlo integration estimates integral : \[\hat{\Omega}_N = \frac{4\pi}{N} \sum_{=1}^{N} \chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x}_i)\] \(\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{=1}^N\) points sampled uniformly \(S^2\), \(4\pi\) total surface area unit sphere.

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Let \(p = \Omega / 4\pi\) true fraction sphere covered \(\mathcal{R}\). estimator \(\hat{p}_N = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{=1}^N \chi_{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{x}_i)\) follows binomial distribution: \[N \hat{p}_N \sim \text{Binomial}(N, p)\] Expected value: \[\mathbb{E}[\hat{\Omega}_N] = 4\pi p = \Omega\] estimator unbiased. Variance: \[\text{Var}(\hat{\Omega}_N) = \frac{(4\pi)^2 p(1-p)}{N} = \frac{16\pi^2 p(1-p)}{N}\] Standard error: \[\text{SE}(\hat{\Omega}_N) = \frac{4\pi\sqrt{p(1-p)}}{\sqrt{N}} = O(N^{-1/2})\] Central Limit Theorem: large \(N\): \[\frac{\hat{\Omega}_N - \Omega}{\text{SE}(\hat{\Omega}_N)} \xrightarrow{d} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\] enables construction confidence intervals: \[\Omega \\left[\hat{\Omega}_N \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \text{SE}(\hat{\Omega}_N)\right]\] \(z_{\alpha/2}\) standard normal quantile (e.g., \(z_{0.025} = 1.96\) 95% confidence).

title: Monte Carlo methods for solid angle computation: convergence, error analysis, and validation
text: Monte Carlo error decreases \(O(N^{-1/2})\), independent dimension. contrasts deterministic quadrature rules, high-dimensional integration suffers “curse dimensionality.” achieve relative error \(\epsilon\), need: \[\frac{\text{SE}}{\Omega} \approx \epsilon \implies N \approx \frac{16\pi^2 p(1-p)}{(\epsilon \Omega)^2} = \frac{(1-p)}{p \epsilon^2}\] \(p = 1/8\) (orthant): \(N \approx 7/\epsilon^2\) 1% accuracy: \(N \approx 70{,}000\) 0.1% accuracy: \(N \approx 7{,}000{,}000\)

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: generation uniformly distributed random vectors spheres within spherical caps fundamental problem computational geometry, statistics, scientific computing. Applications span diverse fields, including Monte Carlo integration spherical domains; directional statistics circular data analysis; computer graphics ray tracing; astrophysics cosmology simulations; molecular dynamics protein folding studies; ecological modeling interaction networks. vignette presents comprehensive treatment sphere sampling methods, emphasis recently developed O(n) algorithm uniform sampling within n-dimensional cones (Arun & Venkatapathi, 2025) [1]. explore historical development sphere sampling techniques; mathematical foundations uniform distributions spheres; classical methods limitations; modern O(n) cone sampling algorithm; rigorous validation statistical testing; practical applications performance comparisons.

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Generating uniform samples full sphere straightforward using Box-Muller transform (Marsaglia, 1972). However, sampling uniformly within spherical cap (base cone) presents fundamental challenges: Naive rejection sampling: cone half-angle \(\theta_0\) n dimensions, acceptance probability solid angle fraction \(\Omega(\theta_0)\). small \(\theta_0\) large n: \[\Omega(\theta_0) \approx \frac{\theta_0^{n-1}}{\sqrt{2\pi e}(n-1)}\] exponential decay makes rejection sampling prohibitively expensive high dimensions. example, 5-degree cone 100 dimensions requires approximately \(10^{150}\) samples per acceptance! O(n) algorithm Arun & Venkatapathi (2025) [1] solves problem generating samples directly within cone using elegant mathematical transformation involving incomplete beta function.
code: 1. Generate point uniformly on full sphere 2. Accept if point lies within cone 3. Otherwise reject and repeat

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Box & Muller (1958) [2] introduced fundamental method generating standard normal random variables, normalized produce uniform distributions spheres. Method: Theorem (Box-Muller): \(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) independent standard normal random variables, \[\hat{x} = \frac{(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_n)}{\sqrt{Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + \cdots + Z_n^2}}\] uniformly distributed unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\).

what: Why the O(n) algorithm is revolutionary
title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: 2025 method solves problem persisted 67 years: sample uniformly within cone without rejection. Previous approaches either used rejection sampling (exponentially inefficient narrow cones); required numerical integration lookup tables (accumulating errors); applied specific geometries (spherical triangles, 3D cones). incomplete beta function approach provides: Mathematical elegance: \[\Theta(\theta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2\theta; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \[0, \frac{\pi}{2}] \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2(\pi - \theta); \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi] \end{cases}\] mapping \(\Theta: [0, \pi] \[0, 1]\) converts complex problem sampling \(f_\theta(\theta) \propto \sin^{n-2}(\theta)\) sampling uniform random variable applying inverse function \(\Theta^{-1}\). Computational efficiency: Numerical stability: algorithm uses log-space calculations incomplete beta function, avoiding underflow even extremely high dimensions (n = 200 tested), narrow cones (θ₀ = 0.001 radians), combined extremes cause \(\Omega_0 < 10^{-100}\). cases inverse transform becomes unstable (n > 80, narrow cones), fallback rejection method log-space ensures robustness.

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: unit sphere \(\mathbb{R}^n\) defined : \[S^{n-1} = \{\mathbf{x} \\mathbb{R}^n : \|\mathbf{x}\| = 1\}\] spherical coordinates, point \(\mathbf{x} \S^{n-1}\) represented using angles \((\phi, \theta_1, \theta_2, \ldots, \theta_{n-2})\) : \(\phi \[0, 2\pi)\) azimuthal angle \(\theta_i \[0, \pi]\) \(= 1, \ldots, n-2\) polar angles Cartesian coordinates : \[\begin{align} x_1 &= \cos\phi \prod_{j=1}^{n-2} \sin\theta_j \\ x_2 &= \sin\phi \prod_{j=1}^{n-2} \sin\theta_j \\ x_k &= \cos\theta_{k-2} \prod_{j=k-1}^{n-2} \sin\theta_j \quad (k = 3, \ldots, n-1) \\ x_n &= \cos\theta_{n-2} \end{align}\]

previous_headings: Mathematical foundations > Spherical coordinates and surface measure
title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: total surface area \(S^{n-1}\) : \[s_n = \frac{2\pi^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)}\] Examples: - \(s_2 = 2\pi\) (circumference circle) - \(s_3 = 4\pi\) (surface 2-sphere) - \(s_4 = 2\pi^2\) (surface 3-sphere) - \(s_5 = \frac{8\pi^2}{3}\) (surface 4-sphere) normalized solid angle region \(\mathcal{R} \subseteq S^{n-1}\) : \[\Omega(\mathcal{R}) = \frac{\text{surface\area}(\mathcal{R})}{s_n}\] \(\Omega \[0, 1]\) represents fraction full sphere.

text: solid angle spherical cap depends planar angle \(\theta_0\) (measured axis) dimension n. Key mapping function: \(\Theta: [0, \pi] \[0, 1]\) \[\Theta(\theta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2\theta; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \[0, \frac{\pi}{2}] \\[10pt] 1 - \frac{1}{2} (\sin^2\theta; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}) & \theta \(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi] \end{cases}\] \((x; \alpha, \beta)\) regularized incomplete beta function: \[(x; \alpha, \beta) = \frac{1}{B(\alpha, \beta)} \int_0^x t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1} dt\]

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: solid angle obtained integrating surface element: \[\Omega(\theta_0) = \frac{1}{s_n} \int_0^{2\pi} \int_0^\pi \cdots \int_0^{\theta_0} \prod_{=1}^{n-2} \sin^\theta_i \, d\theta_{n-2} \cdots d\theta_1 \, d\phi\] Using Wallis integrals relationship beta function: \[\int_0^\theta \sin^m x \, dx = \frac{1}{2} B\left(\frac{m+1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right) \left(\sin^2\theta; \frac{m+1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\] telescoping products simplification, obtain stated formula \(\Theta(\theta)\). Inverse mapping: generation purposes, need \(\Theta^{-1}(\Omega)\): \[\Theta^{-1}(\Omega) = \begin{cases} \arcsin\sqrt{^{-1}(2\Omega; \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})} & \Omega \[0, \frac{1}{2}] \\[10pt] \pi - \arcsin\sqrt{^{-1}(2(1-\Omega); \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{1}{2})} & \Omega \(\frac{1}{2}, 1] \end{cases}\] \(^{-1}\) quantile function beta distribution (available qbeta() R).

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: Given \(\theta_0\), generate \(\theta \[0, \theta_0]\) distribution \(f_\theta\). Method 1 (Inverse transform): 1. Generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \Omega_0)\) \(\Omega_0 = \Theta(\theta_0)\) 2. Return \(\theta = \Theta^{-1}(U)\) Method 2 (Rejection sampling log-space): 1. Generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)\) \(\theta \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \theta_0)\) 2. Accept \(\log U < (n-2)[\log(\sin\theta) - \log(\sin\theta_{\max})]\) 3. Otherwise reject repeat \(\theta_{\max} = \min(\theta_0, \pi/2)\). Advantage Method 2: Numerical stability large n small \(\theta_0\) (avoids underflow \(\Theta\)).

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: rotation \(\hat{e}_n\) \(\hat{\mu}\) performed using Givens rotation 2D plane containing vectors. Construction: Let \(\mu_n = \hat{\mu} \cdot \hat{e}_n\) n-th component \(\hat{\mu}\). Define orthonormal basis \(P\) rotation plane: \[P = \begin{bmatrix} | & | \\ \hat{e}_n & \frac{\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n}{\|\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n\|} \\ | & | \end{bmatrix} \\mathbb{R}^{n \times 2}\] 2D Givens rotation matrix : \[G = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_n & -\sqrt{1-\mu_n^2} \\ \sqrt{1-\mu_n^2} & \mu_n \end{bmatrix}\] rotated vector : \[\hat{y} = \hat{x} + P(G - I_2)P^T\hat{x}\] Complexity: requires O(n) operations (2 dot products, 1 matrix-vector product 2 columns).

title: Uniform Monte Carlo sampling on n-dimensional spheres and spherical caps
text: KS test compares empirical CDF generated angles theoretical CDF. Test statistic: \[D_N = \sup_{\theta \[0, \theta_0]} |\hat{F}_N(\theta) - F_\theta(\theta)|\] null hypothesis (correct distribution), \(\sqrt{N}D_N\) converges Kolmogorov distribution. finite precision, ties can occur sampled angles; apply tiny jitter KS test avoid spurious warnings, consistent verify_cone_uniformity().
code: #### Comprehensive KS test across dimensions and sample sizes            #### dimensions_ks <- c(2, 3, 5, 10, 20) sample_sizes_ks <- c(1000, 5000, 10000, 50000) theta0_ks <- pi/4  ks_results <- expand.grid(   dimension = dimensions_ks,   n_samples = sample_sizes_ks )  ks_results$ks_statistic <- NA ks_results$p_value <- NA  set.seed(42)  for (i in 1:nrow(ks_results)) {   n <- ks_results$dimension[i]   n_samp <- ks_results$n_samples[i]    mu_hat_ks <- c(rep(0, n-1), 1)   samples_ks <- generate_cone_samples(n_samp, mu_hat_ks, theta0_ks)   angles_ks <- acos(samples_ks[n, ])    #### Theoretical CDF                                                   ####   omega0_ks <- theta_to_omega(theta0_ks, n)   theoretical_cdf_ks <- function(theta) {     theta_to_omega(theta, n) / omega0_ks   }    angles_ks_test <- angles_ks   if (any(duplicated(angles_ks_test))) {     angles_ks_test <- jitter(angles_ks_test, amount = max(1e-12, .Machine$double.eps))     angles_ks_test <- pmax(0, pmin(theta0_ks, angles_ks_test))   }   ks_test_result <- ks.test(angles_ks_test, function(x) sapply(x, theoretical_cdf_ks), exact = FALSE)    ks_results$ks_statistic[i] <- as.numeric(ks_test_result$statistic)   ks_results$p_value[i] <- ks_test_result$p.value }  #### Summary statistics                                                  #### pass_rate <- sum(ks_results$p_value > 0.05) / nrow(ks_results) * 100  ks_results$result <- ifelse(ks_results$p_value > 0.05, "\u2714 Pass", "\u2718 Fail") knitr::kable(   ks_results,   digits = c(0, 0, 6, 4, NA),   col.names = c("dimension", "n samples", "KS statistic", "p-value", "result") ) summary_table <- data.frame(   metric = c("Overall pass rate", "Mean KS statistic", "Max KS statistic"),   value = c(     sprintf("%.1f%% (%d / %d)", pass_rate, sum(ks_results$p_value > 0.05), nrow(ks_results)),     sprintf("%.6f", mean(ks_results$ks_statistic)),     sprintf("%.6f", max(ks_results$ks_statistic))   ) ) knitr::kable(summary_table, col.names = c("metric", "value"))

title: Exact analytical solid angles in higher dimensions
text: decades, computing solid angle polyhedral cone dimensions \(n \ge 4\) relied heavily Monte Carlo estimation. closed-form formulas exist \(n=2\) \(n=3\), higher dimensions present significant challenge. normalized solid angle measure \(\tilde{\Omega}_n\) represents probability standard multivariate normal vector falls within cone. statistical contexts, critical calculating orthant probabilities feasibility domains ecological models. SolidAngleR introduces novel capability: exact analytical computation arbitrary dimensions (subject convergence conditions). vignette demonstrates use generalized hypergeometric series method (hypergeometric_series_nd) obtain precise results approximations previously option.

title: Exact analytical solid angles in higher dimensions
text: method based work Ribando (2006) [1], derived multivariable Taylor series expansion solid angle. simplicial cone \(C\) generated unit vectors \(v_1, \dots, v_n\), associated matrix \(M_n(C)\) positive definite, solid angle given : \[ T_{\alpha} = \frac{|\det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum_{\mathbf{}} \left[ \frac{(-2)^{|\mathbf{}|}}{\mathbf{}!} \prod_{=1}^n \Gamma\left(\frac{1 + \text{deg}_i(\mathbf{})}{2}\right) \right] \alpha^{\mathbf{}} \] sum runs multi-indices \(\mathbf{} \\mathbb{N}_0^N\), \(N = \binom{n}{2}\). Implementing general \(n\) non-trivial requires iterating weak compositions integers \(N\) parts. package implements recursive generator solve combinatorial problem dynamically.

title: Exact analytical solid angles in higher dimensions
text: simplest approach solid angles orthogonal cone (orthant). dimension \(n\), normalized solid angle positive orthant exactly \(1/2^n\). can use validate high-dimensional series implementation.  error effectively zero (machine precision), confirming analytical correctness implementation \(n=4, 5, 6\). true power exact method becomes apparent compared Monte Carlo estimation. Monte Carlo unbiased noisy; error decreases slowly \(1/\sqrt{N}\). series method gives “ground truth” Monte Carlo converges. Let’s analyze 5-dimensional cone largely orthogonal satisfies convergence condition (Positive Definite associated matrix).
code: library(SolidAngleR)  dims <- 4:20  results <- data.frame(   Dimension = integer(),   Exact_Theory = numeric(),   Computed_Series = numeric(),   Error = numeric() )  for (n in dims) {   # Orthogonal cone (Identity matrix)   V <- diag(n)      # Compute using the new generic series method   # For orthogonal cones, this is instantaneous as only the 1st term is non-zero   res <- hypergeometric_series_nd(V, tol = 1e-12)      theory <- 1 / 2^n      results <- rbind(results, data.frame(     Dimension = n,     Exact_Theory = theory,     Computed_Series = res$solid_angle,     Error = abs(res$solid_angle - theory)   )) }  # For orthants, the series collapses to the first term, so this table is a # strong sanity check on the n-dimensional implementation. # Print the numeric results table knitr::kable(   results,   digits = c(0, 10, 10, 2),   col.names = c("dimension", "exact theory", "computed series", "abs. error") ) # Set up the plot  # Save current par settings old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) on.exit(par(old_par))  # Set up side-by-side layout (1 row, 2 columns) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)  # Using log="y" because values decay exponentially plot(results$Dimension, results$Exact_Theory,       type = "n",       log = "y",      xlab = "Dimension (n)",       ylab = expression(paste("Normalized solid angle (", omega, ")")),      main = "Computed series vs. Exact theory",      sub = "Simplicial orthogonal cones (Orthants)",      xaxt = "n")  # Custom X axis for integers axis(1, at = dims) grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "lightgray", lty = "dotted")  # 1. Exact Theory: Dark Green Line lines(results$Dimension, results$Exact_Theory,        col = "darkgreen", lwd = 3)  # 2. Computed Series: Orange Points points(results$Dimension, results$Computed_Series,         col = "orange", pch = 19, cex = 1.5)  # Add legend legend("topright",         legend = c("Exact theory (1/2^n)", "Computed series"),        col = c("darkgreen", "orange"),         lty = c(1, NA),         pch = c(NA, 19),         lwd = c(3, NA),        pt.cex = 1.5,        bty = "n")  # Error Trend: Force linear y-axis for error to see machine precision jitter plot(results$Dimension, results$Error,      type = "b", # Both points and lines      col = "red",      pch = 17,   # Triangle point style      lwd = 2,      cex = 1.5,      xlab = "Dimension (n)",      ylab = "Absolute error",      main = "Numerical error trend",      sub = "Floating point precision check",      xaxt = "n")  axis(1, at = dims) grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "lightgray", lty = "dotted")  # Add zero reference line (if errors are distinguishable from 0) abline(h = 0, col = "gray", lty = 2) set.seed(123) n <- 5  # Generate a 5D cone that is Positive Definite # We construct a matrix with small off-diagonal correlations. # For M to be PD, we need sum(|v_i . v_j|) < 1 for each row. # We use a very small off-diagonal value to ensure rapid series convergence # for this demonstration. off_diag <- 0.02 V_5d <- matrix(off_diag, n, n) diag(V_5d) <- 1 V_5d <- normalize_vectors(V_5d)  # Verify PD condition M <- compute_associated_matrix(V_5d) is_pd <- is_positive_definite(M) cat("Is associated matrix Positive Definite?", is_pd, "\n") #> Is associated matrix Positive Definite? TRUE  if (!is_pd) stop("Example cone must be PD for series method!")

title: Exact analytical solid angles in higher dimensions
text: Now run Monte Carlo simulations increasing sample sizes compare estimates exact value.  plot clearly shows Monte Carlo estimates oscillate around true value provided series method. high-precision requirements (e.g., p-values < 0.001), Monte Carlo method require millions samples, whereas series method gives answer instantly.
code: # Define cone test function for general simplicial cone cone_test_func <- function(x) {   # x is in cone if x = V %*% lambda with lambda >= 0   # equivalent to V^(-1) %*% x >= 0   coeffs <- try(solve(V_5d, x), silent = TRUE)   if (inherits(coeffs, "try-error")) return(FALSE)   all(coeffs >= 0) }  # Monte Carlo simulation sample_sizes <- c(1000, 10000, 100000, 500000) mc_estimates <- numeric(length(sample_sizes)) mc_errors <- numeric(length(sample_sizes))  # Use standard rejection sampling on the sphere (robust for general cones) # Note: For very narrow cones, this would be slow, but our cone is wide (~orthant) set.seed(42) for (i in seq_along(sample_sizes)) {   # solid_angle_monte_carlo returns result in steradians (unnormalized)   # We divide by surface area of unit sphere in 5D (8*pi^2/3) to normalize?   # WAIT: solid_angle_monte_carlo uses Marsaglia sampling on sphere and returns:   # Omega = Fraction * SurfaceArea   # Normalized Omega = Omega / SurfaceArea = Fraction      # But solid_angle_monte_carlo result$estimate is UNNORMALIZED (steradians for 3D).   # For generic n, we should implement a custom MC loop or interpret the result correctly.      # Let's implement a direct normalized MC loop here for clarity in n-dimensions   N <- sample_sizes[i]      # Generate N points on 5D sphere   pts <- matrix(rnorm(n * N), nrow = n)   pts <- apply(pts, 2, function(x) x / sqrt(sum(x^2)))      # Check containment   in_cone <- apply(pts, 2, cone_test_func)   count <- sum(in_cone)      p_hat <- count / N   se_hat <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / N)      mc_estimates[i] <- p_hat   mc_errors[i] <- se_hat }  # Plotting plot(log10(sample_sizes), mc_estimates, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "blue",      ylim = range(c(mc_estimates - 2*mc_errors, mc_estimates + 2*mc_errors, true_omega)),      xlab = "log10(Sample Size)", ylab = "Normalized Solid Angle",      main = "Convergence: Exact Series vs. Monte Carlo (5D)")  # Add Error Bars arrows(log10(sample_sizes), mc_estimates - 2*mc_errors,        log10(sample_sizes), mc_estimates + 2*mc_errors,        angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.05, col = "blue")  # Add Exact Reference Line abline(h = true_omega, col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2) legend("topright", c("Monte Carlo Est.", "Exact Series Value"),        col = c("blue", "red"), lty = c(1, 2), pch = c(19, NA))

First, positive definiteness condition requires series converges associated matrix \(M_n(C)\) positive definite; geometrically, means cone “narrow” (vectors highly correlated), condition violated, series diverge produce incorrect results. title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: SolidAngleR package computes normalized solid angle measure polyhedral (simplicial) cones \(\mathbb{R}^n\) arbitrary dimension \(n \geq 2\). computational core implements five distinct algorithmic families, targeting specific class cone geometry: closed-form analytical formulas low dimensions, multivariable hypergeometric series cones positive definite associated matrices, tridiagonal specialization hypergeometric series cones whose Gram matrix banded structure, recursive decomposition method handles fully general case, multivariate normal integration via Quasi-Monte Carlo. vectorized C++ backend (via Rcpp RcppArmadillo) accelerates uniform cone sampling arbitrary dimensions. document describes mathematical foundations, numerical algorithms, software architecture, complete API surface package.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Given \(n\) linearly independent vectors \(v_1, \ldots, v_n \\mathbb{R}^n\), simplicial cone \(C = \text{cone}(v_1, \ldots, v_n) = \{\sum_{=1}^n \lambda_i v_i : \lambda_i \geq 0\}\) traces region unit sphere \(S^{n-1}\). normalized solid angle measure \(\omega(C) \[0, 1]\) fraction \(S^{n-1}\) covered \(C\): \[ \omega(C) = \frac{\text{vol}_{n-1}(C \cap S^{n-1})}{\text{vol}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})} \] positive orthant \(C = \{x \\mathbb{R}^n : x_i \geq 0\}\), \(\omega(C) = 1/2^n\). methods package return normalized measure.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Central package associated matrix \(M_n(C)\) (Definition 1.1 Fitisone & Zhou [1]), constructed unit generators \(\hat{v}_i = v_i / \|v_i\|\): \[ M_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{} = j \\ -|\hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_j| & \text{} \neq j \end{cases} \] positive definiteness \(M_n(C)\) determines whether hypergeometric series converges (Theorem 1.5 [1]). package computes \(M_n(C)\) via compute_associated_matrix() tests positive definiteness eigendecomposition tolerance \(\epsilon = 10^{-10}\).

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Two dimensions. \(v_1, v_2 \\mathbb{R}^2\), solid angle planar angle rays, normalized \(2\pi\): \[ \omega = \frac{1}{2\pi} \arctan2\!\left(|\det[v_1, v_2]|,\; v_1 \cdot v_2\right) \] implementation uses atan2 correct quadrant handling returns 0 collinear opposite vectors. Colinear detection uses tolerance \(10^{-15}\) determinant magnitude. Implementation: R/formulas_2d.R exports solid_angle_2d(v1, v2). Three dimensions. \(v_1, v_2, v_3 \\mathbb{R}^3\), Euler-Lagrange formula [2] computes spherical excess: \[ E = 2\,\arctan2\!\left(\left|v_1 \cdot (v_2 \times v_3)\right|,\; 1 + v_1 \cdot v_2 + v_1 \cdot v_3 + v_2 \cdot v_3\right) \] \(\omega = E / (4\pi)\). numerator absolute value scalar triple product; denominator handles case \(1 + \sum \text{dot products} < 0\) atan2 branch cut. triple product smaller \(10^{-15}\), cone degenerate function returns 0. Implementation: R/formulas_3d.R exports solid_angle_3d(v1, v2, v3), solid_angle_3d_det(V) (matrix interface), spherical_triangle_area(v1, v2, v3) (returns \(E\) steradians rather normalized measure).

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: \(n \geq 4\) \(M_n(C)\) positive definite, Ribando’s multivariable hypergeometric series [3] computes solid angle power series pairwise dot products \(\alpha_{ij} = \hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_j\): \[ \omega(C) = \frac{|\det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum_{\mathbf{} \\mathbb{N}_0^N} \left[ \frac{(-2)^{|\mathbf{}|}}{\mathbf{}!} \prod_{=1}^n \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1 + \deg_i(\mathbf{})}{2}\right) \right] \boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{}} \] \(N = \binom{n}{2}\) number distinct pairs, \(\mathbf{} = (a_{12}, a_{13}, \ldots, a_{n-1,n})\) multi-index exponents, \(|\mathbf{}| = \sum a_{jk}\) total degree, \(\mathbf{}! = \prod a_{jk}!\), \(\deg_i(\mathbf{}) = \sum_{k \neq } a_{ik}\) degree vertex \(\) multigraph defined \(\mathbf{}\), \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{\mathbf{}} = \prod \alpha_{jk}^{a_{jk}}\). series converges absolutely \(M_n(C)\) positive definite. Convergence speed depends eigenvalue spread: nearly orthogonal cones (\(\alpha_{ij} \approx 0\)) converge terms, cones large dot products require many terms even \(M_n(C)\) positive definite. Algorithmic strategy. implementation enumerates multi-indices total degree \(d = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\), generating weak compositions \(d\) \(N\) parts via recursive backtracking. degree, degree contribution accumulated, convergence declared absolute change consecutive degrees falls tol. Specialized implementations \(n = 2\) (single-variable series \(\alpha_{12}\)) \(n = 3\) (three-variable series \(\alpha_{12}, \alpha_{13}, \alpha_{23}\)) avoid overhead general partition enumeration. Complexity. number weak compositions \(d\) \(N\) parts \(\binom{d + N - 1}{N - 1}\), grows combinatorially \(d\) \(N\). \(n \geq 5\) becomes expensive, though convergence typically occurs low \(d\) well-conditioned cones. Implementation: R/series_hypergeometric.R exports hypergeometric_series(V, max_terms, tol, check_pd) dispatcher, hypergeometric_series_nd(V, max_terms, tol) general \(n\)-dimensional engine, internal helpers hypergeometric_series_2d(), hypergeometric_series_3d(), compute_series_term_3d().

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Gram matrix \(V^T V\) tridiagonal (.e., \(\hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_j = 0\) \(|- j| > 1\)), hypergeometric series simplifies dramatically. summation reduces \(N = \binom{n}{2}\) variables \(n - 1\) consecutive dot products \(\beta_i = \hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_{+1}\): \[ \omega(C) = \frac{|\det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum_{\mathbf{b} \\mathbb{N}_0^{n-1}} \left[ \frac{(-2)^{|\mathbf{b}|}}{\mathbf{b}!}\, \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1+b_1}{2}\right) \prod_{=2}^{n-1} \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1+b_{-1}+b_i}{2}\right) \Gamma\!\left(\frac{1+b_{n-1}}{2}\right) \right] \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathbf{b}} \] Theorem 4.1 [1], tridiagonality \(V^T V\) implies \(M_n(C)\) automatically positive definite, series always converges. reduced dimensionality (\(n - 1\) instead \(\binom{n}{2}\)) yields substantial computational advantage, particularly high dimensions. Implementation: R/series_tridiagonal.R exports tridiagonal_series(V, max_terms, tol) internal compute_tridiagonal_term(b, beta). multi-index enumeration uses generate_partitions(n, k) R/utils.R.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: \(M_n(C)\) positive definite, hypergeometric series converge. decomposition method, based Brion-Vergne theory [1], recursively partitions cone sub-cones, either positive definite associated matrix affine dimension less \(n\) (contributing zero solid angle). Algorithm. Given generators \(V = [v_1, \ldots, v_n]\): \(M_n(C)\) already positive definite, return \(V\) single terminal cone. Compute \(\delta_i = \text{sign}(\hat{v}_i \cdot \hat{v}_n)\) \(= 1, \ldots, n-1\). \(\delta_i = 0\) (\(\hat{v}_n\) orthogonal generators), project onto \((n-1)\)-dimensional subspace orthogonal \(\hat{v}_n\) recurse. Otherwise, \(\) \(\delta_i \neq 0\), construct decomposed cone \(C_i\) generators: \[ u_{,k} = \begin{cases} v_k & \text{} \delta_k = 0 \text{ } k = \\ \epsilon_{ik}\left(v_k - \frac{v_k \cdot v_n}{v_i \cdot v_n} v_i\right) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \] \(\epsilon_{ik}\) sign factor Equation 15 [1]. \(C_i\) carries sign \(s_i = \pm 1\) computed delta sequence. solid angle original cone \(\omega(C) = \sum_i s_i \cdot \omega(C_i)\). Recurse sub-cone whose associated matrix still positive definite. Corollary 3.4, decomposition produces \((n-1)!\) terminal cones. worst-case complexity therefore \(O(2^n)\), though well-conditioned cones typically decompose far fewer pieces. Implementation: R/decomposition.R exports decompose_cone(V, method), solid_angle_decomposition(V, max_terms, tol), internal helpers decompose_by_line(V), compute_epsilon(, k, delta).

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Ribando’s approach [3] reformulates solid angle probability multivariate normal random variable falls positive orthant transformed coordinate system: \[ \omega(C) = \int_{\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n} \phi_n(\mathbf{x};\, \mathbf{0},\, \Sigma)\, d\mathbf{x} \] \(\Sigma = (V^T V)^{-1}\) \(\phi_n\) \(n\)-dimensional Gaussian density. algorithm computes \(B = V^T V\), inverts obtain \(\Sigma\), evaluates integral via mvtnorm::pmvnorm(), uses Genz-Bretz Quasi-Monte Carlo algorithm [4] Halton sequences importance sampling. method works cone \(B\) positive definite, provides results exact numerical integration tolerance, avoids combinatorial explosion hypergeometric series. However, matrix inversion becomes ill-conditioned large \(n\) nearly dependent generators; function warns \(\kappa(B) > 10^{10}\) unreliable \(n > 20\). Complexity: \(O(n^3)\) matrix inversion plus \(O(M \times n^2)\) Quasi-Monte Carlo integration, \(M\) number adaptive quadrature points. Implementation: R/omega.R exports omega(alpha), returning raw measure geometric mean per dimension \(\omega^{1/n}\).

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: package provides specialized formulas geometrically defined cones \(\mathbb{R}^3\) bypass general-purpose machinery. Right circular cones. Mazonka formula [5] (Equation 9) gives normalized solid angle cone apex half-angle \(\theta\): \[ \omega = \frac{2\pi(1 - \cos\theta)}{4\pi} = \frac{1 - \cos\theta}{2} \] Implementation: solid_angle_cone(theta) R/geometric_methods.R. Polyhedral cones (spherical polygons). Van Oosterom-Strackee formula [2] computes solid angle spherical triangle defined three unit vectors \(v_1, v_2, v_3\): \[ \tan\!\left(\frac{\Omega}{2}\right) = \frac{|v_1 \cdot (v_2 \times v_3)|}{1 + v_1 \cdot v_2 + v_1 \cdot v_3 + v_2 \cdot v_3} \] spherical polygons \(n > 3\) vertices, function decomposes triangular fans first vertex sums contributions. Implementation: solid_angle_polyhedral(vertices) R/geometric_methods.R. Cone segments. cone segment portion circular cone cut plane angle \(\gamma\) axis. Mazonka formula [5] (Equations 35, 39, 41) computes auxiliary angles: \[ \phi = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\cos\gamma}{\tan\theta}\right), \qquad \beta = \arccos\!\left(\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\theta}\right) \] solid angle \(\Omega = 2(\phi - \cos\theta \cdot \beta)\), normalized \(4\pi\). analytic expression yields negative invalid value, function falls back numerical integration spherical-cap intersection via stats::integrate() 2000 subdivisions. Implementation: solid_angle_cone_segment(theta, gamma) R/geometric_methods.R. Intersecting cones. two circular cones half-angles \(\theta_1\), \(\theta_2\) axis separation \(\alpha\), intersection solid angle computed numerical integration azimuthally admissible arc length: \[ \Omega = \int_0^{\theta_1} L(\theta)\,\sin\theta\,d\theta \] \(L(\theta) = 2\arccos C(\theta)\) \(C(\theta) = (\cos\theta_2 - \cos\alpha\cos\theta)/(\sin\alpha\sin\theta)\), clamped \([-1, 1]\). Special cases (overlap, containment, co-directed axes, opposite axes, hemisphere intersections) handled analytically falling back integration. Implementation: solid_angle_intersecting_cones(theta1, theta2, alpha, method, fallback, mc_samples, mc_seed) R/geometric_methods.R. L’Huilier’s theorem. spherical excess triangle arc-length sides \(, b, c\) : \[ E = 4\arctan\sqrt{\tan\!\left(\frac{s}{2}\right)\tan\!\left(\frac{s-}{2}\right)\tan\!\left(\frac{s-b}{2}\right)\tan\!\left(\frac{s-c}{2}\right)} \] \(s = (+ b + c)/2\). provides numerically stable alternative Girard’s theorem \(E = \alpha + \beta + \gamma - \pi\). Implementation: lhuilier_angle(, b, c) R/extreme_rays.R.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: package implements \(O(n)\) algorithm Arun & Venkatapathi [6] generating points uniformly distributed spherical cap (intersection cone \(S^{n-1}\)) arbitrary dimension.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: function \(\Theta: [0, \pi] \[0, 1]\) maps planar half-angle \(\theta\) fraction sphere enclosed corresponding cone: \[ \Theta(\theta) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2}\,\!\left(\sin^2\theta;\, \frac{n-1}{2},\, \frac{1}{2}\right) & \theta \\left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right] \\ 1 - \frac{1}{2}\,\!\left(\sin^2\theta;\, \frac{n-1}{2},\, \frac{1}{2}\right) & \theta \\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right] \end{cases} \] \((x; \alpha, \beta)\) regularized incomplete beta function, computed via pbeta(). inverse \(\Theta^{-1}\) uses qbeta(). piecewise definition avoids catastrophic cancellation near \(\theta = \pi/2\). Implementation: theta_to_omega(theta, n) omega_to_theta(omega, n) R/cone_sampling.R.

title: Technical architecture and API reference
text: Given cone axis \(\hat{\mu} \S^{n-1}\) half-angle \(\theta_0\), uniformly distributed point spherical cap generated four steps: Step 1. Generate random planar angle. Sample \(\theta \[0, \theta_0]\) distribution \(F_\theta(\theta) = \Theta(\theta) / \Theta(\theta_0)\). Two methods available: Inverse transform sampling: generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \Theta(\theta_0))\) return \(\theta = \Theta^{-1}(U)\). Fast vulnerable floating-point underflow large \(n\) small \(\theta_0\). 1D rejection sampling: generate \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\) \(\theta \sim \text{Uniform}(0, \theta_0)\); accept \(\log U < (n-2)[\log\sin\theta - \log\sin\min(\theta_0, \pi/2)]\). log transform prevents underflow. Expected number rejections \(O(n)\), maintaining overall \(O(n)\) complexity. Step 2. Generate perpendicular component. Sample \(\hat{x}_\perp\) uniformly \(S^{n-2}\) using Marsaglia method [7]: draw \(z_1, \ldots, z_{n-1} \sim N(0, 1)\) normalize. -loop rejects samples \(\|\mathbf{z}\| < 10^{-15}\). Step 3. Construct canonical vector. Form \(\hat{x} = (\sin\theta \cdot \hat{x}_\perp,\; \cos\theta)\) aligned \(n\)-th canonical basis vector \(\hat{e}_n\). Step 4. Rotate target orientation. Apply Givens rotation plane containing \(\hat{e}_n\) \(\hat{\mu}\): \[ \hat{y} = \hat{x} + P(G - I_2)P^T\hat{x} \] \(P = [\hat{e}_n,\; (\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n)/\|\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n\|]\) \(n \times 2\) orthonormal basis rotation plane \(G\) \(2 \times 2\) Givens matrix: \[ G = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_n & -\sqrt{1 - \mu_n^2} \\ \sqrt{1 - \mu_n^2} & \mu_n \end{bmatrix} \] rotation costs \(O(n)\) operations (two dot products two vector additions), unlike general \(n\)-dimensional rotation matrix cost \(O(n^2)\). Edge cases. \(\hat{\mu}\) nearly parallel \(\hat{e}_n\) (\(|1 - \mu_n^2| < 10^{-10}\)), second column \(P\) set zero, rotation reduces identity (parallel) reflection (antiparallel). implementation guards negative arguments sqrt via max(0, 1 - \mu_n^2). Hollow cones. algorithm extends annular regions \(\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2\) sampling \(U \sim \text{Uniform}(\Theta(\theta_1), \Theta(\theta_2))\) applying \(\theta = \Theta^{-1}(U)\). Implementation (R): R/cone_sampling.R exports generate_cone_sample(), generate_cone_samples(), generate_hollow_cone_sample(), generate_planar_angle_inverse(), generate_planar_angle_rejection(), rotate_from_canonical(), generate_point_on_sphere(), rejection_cost(), verify_cone_uniformity().

title: Computing normalized solid angles of polyhedral cones in arbitrary dimensions
text: normalized solid angle measure \(\tilde{\Omega}_n(C)\) polyhedral cone \(C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) quantifies proportion \(n\)-dimensional space occupied cone. Formally: \[\tilde{\Omega}_n(C) = \frac{\text{vol}_{n-1}(C \cap S^{n-1})}{\text{vol}_{n-1}(S^{n-1})}\] \(S^{n-1}\) unit sphere \(\mathbb{R}^n\). 2D (\(n=2\)), \(\tilde{\Omega}_2 = \frac{\theta}{2\pi}\), \(\theta\) planar angle radians. 3D (\(n=3\)), \(\tilde{\Omega}_3 = \frac{\Omega}{4\pi}\), \(\Omega\) standard solid angle steradians. n-D, \(\tilde{\Omega}_n\) represents fraction unit hypersphere surface covered cone.

title: Computing normalized solid angles of polyhedral cones in arbitrary dimensions
text: normalized solid angle several fundamental properties. range \(\tilde{\Omega}_n(C) \[0, 1]\); orthant (axes-aligned cone), \(\tilde{\Omega}_n(\mathbb{R}^n_{\geq 0}) = \frac{1}{2^n}\); full space, \(\tilde{\Omega}_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = 1\); empty cone, \(\tilde{\Omega}_n(\emptyset) = 0\).

title: Compute normalized solid angle measure of a polyhedral cone — compute_solid_angle
text: function implements multiple methods Fitisone & Zhou (2023): n = 2: Uses angle formula: \(\Omega = \theta/(2\pi)\) n = 3: Uses Euler-Lagrange formula: $$E = 2 \arctan\left(\frac{|v_1 \cdot (v_2 \times v_3)|}{1 + v_2 \cdot v_3 + v_2 \cdot v_1 + v_1 \cdot v_3}\right)$$ \(\Omega = E/(4\pi)\) n \(\geq\) 4 positive definite associated matrix: Uses Ribando's hypergeometric series (Theorem 1.5) n \(\geq\) 4 tridiagonal structure: Uses simplified series n-1 coordinates (Theorem 4.1) general case: Uses decomposition method (Theorems 3.3 Corollary 3.4)

title: General n-dimensional hypergeometric series for solid angle — hypergeometric_series_nd
text: Mathematical Formulation: function computes series: $$T_{\alpha} = \frac{|\det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum_{\mathbf{} \\mathbb{N}_0^N} \left[ \frac{(-2)^{|\mathbf{}|}}{\mathbf{}!} \prod_{=1}^n \Gamma\left(\frac{1 + \text{deg}_i(\mathbf{})}{2}\right) \right] \alpha^{\mathbf{}}$$ \(N = \binom{n}{2}\) number pairwise dot products; \(\mathbf{} = (a_{12}, a_{13}, \dots, a_{n-1,n})\) multi-index exponents; \(|\mathbf{}| = \sum_{j<k} a_{jk}\) total degree term; \(\text{deg}_i(\mathbf{}) = \sum_{k \ne } a_{ik}\) "degree" vertex \(\) multigraph defined \(\mathbf{}\). Algorithmic Strategy: Unlike hardcoded implementations \(n=3\), function dynamically generates multi-indices \(\mathbf{}\) increasing total degrees \(d = 0, 1, 2, \dots\). uses recursive backtracking algorithm find weak compositions \(d\) \(N\) parts. Performance Limitations: Regarding convergence, series converges absolutely associated matrix \(M_n(C)\) positive definite, typically means cone vectors must close (cone must narrow); condition violated, series may produce meaningless results fail converge. terms computational complexity, number terms grows combinatorially \(n\) degree \(d\), \(n \ge 5\), calculating high-degree terms becomes computationally expensive. Convergence speed varies substantially: cones nearly orthogonal (dot products close 0), convergence fast, whereas cones high correlation generators (even positive definite), convergence can slow may require many terms achieve high precision; cases, Monte Carlo methods might efficient.

title: Calculate solid angle of spherical triangle using L'Huilier's theorem — lhuilier_angle
text: Given spherical triangle side lengths \(\), \(b\), \(c\) (measured great circle arcs radians), solid angle \(E\) : $$\tan\left(\frac{E}{4}\right) = \sqrt{\tan\left(\frac{s}{2}\right) \tan\left(\frac{s-}{2}\right) \tan\left(\frac{s-b}{2}\right) \tan\left(\frac{s-c}{2}\right)}$$ \(s = (+ b + c)/2\) semi-perimeter. Solving \(E\): $$E = 4 \arctan\left(\sqrt{\tan\left(\frac{s}{2}\right) \tan\left(\frac{s-}{2}\right) \tan\left(\frac{s-b}{2}\right) \tan\left(\frac{s-c}{2}\right)}\right)$$

title: Compute normalized solid angle via multivariate normal integration — omega
text: Mathematical foundation (Theorem 2.2 Ribando 2006): normalized solid angle measure defined : $$\tilde{V}_{\omega} = \frac{\int_{\omega} f \, dx}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f \, dx}$$ \(f = e^{-r^2}\) \(r = |x|\). change coordinates application Gaussian integral, reduces integrating zero-mean multivariate normal distribution covariance matrix \(\Sigma = B^{-1}\) positive orthant \(\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^n\). Characteristics algorithm: algorithm proceeds follows: Compute \(B = \alpha^T \alpha\) Compute \(\Sigma = B^{-1}\) (requires B positive definite) Integrate \(N(0, \Sigma)\) \([0, \infty)^n\) mvtnorm::pmvnorm(), uses Genz-Bretz algorithm (Genz & Bretz 2009). Genz-Bretz algorithm implements Quasi-Monte Carlo integration Halton sequences, uses importance sampling reduce variance, provides adaptive subdivision high-dimensional integrals, estimates error via repeated evaluations. Convergence: algorithm works cone associated matrix B positive definite. provides exact (numerical integration tolerance) result without requiring series convergence. However, matrix ill-conditioned /matrix dimension large (>20) results may unreliable. Complexity Matrix inversion: \(O(n^3)\) mvtnorm::pmvnorm(): \(O(M \times n^2)\) M number integration points Total: \(O(n^3 + M \times n^2)\)

title: Rotate vector from n-th canonical basis to arbitrary orientation — rotate_from_canonical
text: function performs Givens rotation plane containing \(\hat{e}_n\) \(\hat{\mu}\). rotation : $$\hat{y} = \hat{x} + P(G - I_2)P^T\hat{x}$$ P orthonormal basis plane rotation, G 2D Givens rotation matrix, \(I_2\) 2×2 identity matrix. matrices defined : $$P = [\hat{e}_n, \frac{\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n}   {\|\hat{\mu} - \mu_n\hat{e}_n\|}]$$ $$G = \begin{bmatrix} \mu_n & -\sqrt{1-\mu_n^2} \\   \sqrt{1-\mu_n^2} & \mu_n \end{bmatrix}$$ \(\mu_n = \hat{e}_n^T\hat{\mu}\). rotation costs O(n) operations, unlike general n-dimensional rotations cost O(n²).

title: Compute solid angle of a cone segment — solid_angle_cone_segment
text: cone segment portion circular cone cut plane. solid angle depends cone's apex angle \(\theta\) cutting plane's orientation \(\gamma\). calculation uses auxiliary angles (Equations 35, 39, 41 Mazonka 2012): $$\phi = \arccos\left(\frac{\cos\gamma}{\tan\theta}\right)$$ $$\beta = \arccos\left(\frac{\sin\gamma}{\sin\theta}\right)$$ $$\Omega = 2(\phi - \cos\theta \cdot \beta)$$ analytic expression yields negative invalid value due numerical issues boundary geometry, function falls back robust numerical integration equivalent spherical-cap intersection. Special cases handled automatically: \(\gamma = 0\), function returns full cone solid angle; \(\gamma > \pi/2 + \theta\), plane misses cone entirely function returns 0; \(\phi\) \(\beta\) invalid, geometric constraints prevent intersection.

text: function implements decomposition method based Theorem 3.3 Corollary 3.4 Ribando (2006). method handles general case Gram matrix \(M = V^T V\) positive-definite. Algorithm: Check cone 2D 3D positive-definite Gram matrix. , use direct hypergeometric formulas Otherwise, decompose cone recursively using Theorem 3.3: $$\text{cone}(V) = \text{cone}(V_{n-1}) \cup \bigcup_{=1}^{n-1} (-1)^\text{cone}(V_{[]})$$ \(V_{n-1}\) first \(n-1\) columns \(V_{[]}\) replaces column \(\) last column Compute solid angles decomposed cone (PD matrices) using hypergeometric series: solid_angle_2d solid_angle_3d Sum signed contributions according inclusion-exclusion principle Mathematical background: simplicial cone \(\mathbb{R}^n\) defined vectors \(V = [v_1, \ldots, v_n]\), solid angle measure spherical region traced unit sphere. Gram matrix positive-definite, hypergeometric series provide exact computation. PD, decomposition reduces problem PD subcones. recursion terminates subcones PD Gram matrices, guaranteeing convergence. However, random configurations, deep recursion may cause stack overflow (see package limitations NEWS.md). use: method appropriate Gram matrix \(M = V^T V\) positive-definite, methods fail applicable, theoretical verification methods required. Performance: Computational complexity \(O(2^n)\) worst case due recursive decomposition, typically much faster well-conditioned cones.

") #> 3D orthogonal cone (octant): 0.125 should be 1/8 = 0.125   # Example 3: 3D cone requiring decomposition (non-PD Gram matrix) set.seed(123) V3_npd <- matrix(rnorm(9), nrow = 3) V3_npd <- normalize_vectors(V3_npd)  M <- compute_associated_matrix(V3_npd) cat("Is Gram matrix PD?", is_positive_definite(M), "

") #> 3D non-PD cone solid angle: 0.0562723   if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Example 4: Compare decomposition with direct method V <- matrix(c(   1, 1, 1,   -1, 1, 1,   0, 0, 1 ), nrow = 3, byrow = TRUE) V <- normalize_vectors(V)  # Check if we can use direct method M <- compute_associated_matrix(V) if (is_positive_definite(M)) {   omega_direct <- solid_angle_3d(V[, 1], V[, 2], V[, 3])   omega_decomp <- solid_angle_decomposition(V)   cat("Direct method:", omega_direct, "
")   cat("Decomposition:", omega_decomp, "
")   cat("Difference:", abs(omega_direct - omega_decomp), "
") } else {   cat("Gram matrix not PD, using decomposition
")   omega_decomp <- solid_angle_decomposition(V)   cat("Result:", omega_decomp, "
") } } # }

title: Compute solid angle of intersection of two cones — solid_angle_intersecting_cones
text: intersection two circular cones corresponds intersection two spherical caps unit sphere. coordinate system first axis north pole second axis separated angle \(\alpha\), point sphere $$x(\theta,\varphi) = (\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\; \sin\theta\sin\varphi,\; \cos\theta)$$ belongs second cone $$\sin\alpha \sin\theta \cos\varphi + \cos\alpha \cos\theta \ge \cos\theta_2.$$ \(\theta \[0,\theta_1]\), admissible azimuth range $$\varphi \[-\arccos C(\theta),\, \arccos C(\theta)]$$ $$C(\theta) = \frac{\cos\theta_2 - \cos\alpha \cos\theta}{\sin\alpha \sin\theta}.$$ solid angle (steradians) intersection $$\Omega = \int_0^{\theta_1} L(\theta)\,\sin\theta\,d\theta$$ \(L(\theta)\) admissible azimuth length. result normalized \(4\pi\). methods handle several special cases: overlap (\(\alpha \ge \theta_1 + \theta_2\)), function returns 0; one cone contains (\(\alpha \le |\theta_1 - \theta_2|\)), returns smaller cone; co-directed axes (\(\alpha \approx 0\)), returns smaller cone; opposite axes (\(\alpha \approx \pi\)), uses closed-form band area; two hemispheres intersect, returns \((\pi - \alpha)/(2\pi)\); one cone hemisphere, reduces solid_angle_cone_segment \(\gamma = \alpha\).

title: Compute solid angle using tridiagonal hypergeometric series — tridiagonal_series
text: formula (equation 23) tridiagonal \(V^T V\) : $$T_{\beta} = \frac{|det V|}{(4\pi)^{n/2}} \sum \left[ \frac{(-2)^{\sum b_i}}{\prod b_i!} \Gamma\left(\frac{1+b_1}{2}\right) \Gamma\left(\frac{1+b_1+b_2}{2}\right) \cdots \Gamma\left(\frac{1+b_{n-2}+b_{n-1}}{2}\right) \Gamma\left(\frac{1+b_{n-1}}{2}\right) \right] \beta^b$$ \(\beta_i = v_i \cdot v_{+1}\) \(= 1, \ldots, n-1\). Theorem 4.1, V^T V tridiagonal, associated matrix automatically positive definite, series always converges.
